Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Therapy Content: avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Vignette:
### Clinical Vignette for Ethan Ethan is a 19-year-old European American male who works as a counselor and has been struggling with symptoms following a life-threatening illness. His trauma began when he was admitted to the hospital after experiencing severe complications from his condition. The experience of being hooked up to medical equipment, the constant monitoring, and the fear of death left deep scars that continue to haunt him. In the immediate aftermath of his discharge, Ethan found himself unable to return home without feeling anxious about any reminders of the hospital environment. Simple things like the antiseptic smell or seeing a needle would trigger intense reactions. He had come to believe that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore and that his body could no longer be trusted. The physical sensations he experienced during his illness were now interpreted as signs of danger, even though they occurred in safe environments. Ethan's avoidance behaviors developed gradually over time. Initially, it was a way for him to cope with the overwhelming anxiety and fear. He started by avoiding any medical procedures or hospitals altogether. This meant that he would skip routine check-ups and avoid anything that could be remotely associated with his traumatic experience. For instance, when his girlfriend suggested they visit a hospital for a minor issue, Ethan’s reaction was one of extreme distress and panic. His work as a counselor also became challenging due to these triggers. He had come to believe that thinking about the therapy content would lead him back into those terrifying moments in the hospital. As a result, he started avoiding deep discussions or topics related to his illness during therapy sessions. This pattern led to a decline in his performance at work and a growing sense of disconnection from his professional role. Ethan’s sleep patterns were also significantly affected. He found it increasingly difficult to fall asleep due to the intrusive thoughts and images associated with his trauma. When he did manage to sleep, any sudden movement or noise would jolt him awake, convinced that danger was imminent. The startle response became so severe that even normal interactions in his daily life felt like threats. The avoidance of therapy content extended to other areas of his life. He began staying up very late at night as a way to distract himself from these distressing thoughts and memories. This led to significant disruptions in his routine, affecting both his work performance and personal relationships. His girlfriend noticed the changes but found it hard to understand why he was becoming so distant. Ethan’s most recent trigger occurred during an annual health fair at his workplace where medical professionals were on-site for basic examinations. The sight of the medical equipment triggered a full-blown panic attack, leaving him feeling trapped and unable to breathe. This incident was the final push that brought Ethan into therapy. He realized he could no longer continue living in this state of constant fear and avoidance. When asked about his fears and hopes for treatment, Ethan expressed deep concerns about whether he would ever feel safe again or if he could regain a sense of control over his body and life. Despite these fears, there was also a palpable hope that through therapy, he might find some relief from the overwhelming anxiety and start to reconnect with his previous sense of self. Ethan’s current state is one of both desperation and cautious optimism as he seeks help to navigate his traumatic experience and its aftermath. The underlying belief that his body is untrustworthy and a constant source of danger remains a significant barrier, but Ethan hopes that therapy will provide him with the tools to regain some control over his life and relationships.
